title: Festival Committee Webinar: Sharing Skills Beyond the Stage
notice: Synthetic demo material. Invented document; no real meeting, publication, email or call occurred.

blocks.text: Hello everyone, and welcome. Rowan Bell here, community manager for the Leadership Network. I see we have a full house tonight from all the countries. Wonderful. This is one of our themed check-ins, and September’s focus is the Festival Committee. But as you know, the threads that make up our festivals—craft, food, music, care—run through everything we do in our circles. Tonight we have a few members joining to talk about recent projects and plans that, to me, feel like they have that same festival spirit, even if they happened in a workshop, a kitchen, or a clinic. They’ve each got a few minutes to share, and then we’ll open it up. Oriel, let’s start with you.

Thank you, Rowan. This is Oriel Brambleworth, from the Green Market. The festival giant—the one we use in the autumn parade—was in a bit of a state after last year. The control lines, the ones that let you make it wave and bow, had frayed badly. It’s always a tricky job; the lines need strength, but they can’t be so stiff that they fight the puppet’s movement. I’d been mulling it over for months. Then, on a trip to the Quadling lakes, I saw an angler using a new braided fishing line. Incredibly strong for its width, and supple. I had a thought. I got some, spent three days re-threading the entire control harness. The difference is night and day. The puppet moves more fluidly now, and I don’t have that constant worry of a line snapping mid-parade. Not much to look at, but it’s like finding the right joint for a marionette—it lets the character live properly.
A perfect example of a solution from an unexpected place. Thank you, Oriel. Flora, you’re up next in Reed Flats.

Hello, Flora Hayworth here. Listening to Oriel talk about preparation for the big event makes me think of my own pantry! My plan for this autumn is much smaller in scale but, I hope, just as useful. I’m going to host three preserving workshops in my kitchen here. We get such a glut of turnips, beets, and the last of the orchard fruits. The idea is to show folks how to pickle the roots so they’re not just eating boiled turnips all winter, and how to make a good, spicy chutney that’ll brighten up a plate. It’s not formal catering, just neighbors and friends rolling up their sleeves. If anyone from the network is in the Reed Flats area and wants to come, let me know. We’ll set the dates once the first frost hits the gardens.
That’s a lovely offer, Flora. A different kind of sustenance. Now, Ines, from Redfern Hill. You had a different kind of community care project.

Yes, hello. Ines Emeryby. I’m a dental hygienist. This wasn’t for a festival, but it was about making something accessible. We kept hearing from patients who worked the late shifts at the timber mill or in security—they just couldn’t get to a routine cleaning during our normal hours. It was always ‘I’ll try next year.’ So, we added one late evening session a week. Just one hygienist, me, and the dentist on call. It’s quiet, and it’s made all the difference for those few people. One man came in last week and said it was the first time in a decade he hadn’t used a vacation day just to see the dentist. It’s a small adjustment, but it matters.
It absolutely does. Thank you, Ines. Rosa, I understand you had a repair project that turned into something beautiful?

That’s right, Rosa Clay from Clay Hollow. In our studio, we have a massive old mixing bowl for glazes. It’s practically an heirloom, and it developed a nasty crack. Everyone was ready to retire it. But I remembered reading about the Quadling art of repair, the art of repairing with gold. I thought, why not try the spirit of it? I used a food-safe epoxy mixed with a very fine gold powder. It took patience to align the pieces and apply the mix cleanly—no messy wedging here! Now the bowl is whole again, and the crack is highlighted with this delicate gold line. It’s still a workhorse for mixing, but it also tells a story. It’s a reminder that things don’t have to be thrown away. They can be mended, and the mending can add to their value.
A wonderful philosophy. And finally, Alma, bringing us back to music.

Alma Reedton, from the Heatherford Brass Band. My project was very, very small, but in a band, every instrument matters. Our second cornet player has a vintage mouthpiece he loves, but the thread that screws it onto the lead pipe was completely stripped. You’d get a note, and then—pfft—it would come loose. A new one wouldn’t feel the same to him. So I borrowed a miniature tap-and-die set from a clock repair friend. It took a steady hand and a lot of deep breaths to re-cut that tiny thread without damaging the piece. When it screwed on snugly again, the smile on his face was better than a standing ovation. It’s fixed now. The band sounds whole because one person isn’t worrying his mouthpiece will fly off during the march.
From giant puppets to tiny threads. Thank you all. Now, let’s open the floor. Who has a question or a comment about what they’ve heard?
This is Marlow, from the Brickway Transit circle. A question for Oriel. That braided line—is it affected by damp? The autumn parade can be a bit drizzly.

A good question. I tested it. Left a length soaking in a bucket for a week. No loss of strength, no stretching that I could measure. It’s designed for water, after all. Should hold up better than the old linen cords we used.
And Flora, for your workshops, will you provide the jars, or should people bring their own?
I’ll have a few spares, but if you have a favorite jar with a good seal, bring it along. We’ll talk about how to sterilize them properly, too. It’s all part of the process.
Ines, has the late session been busy? Are you thinking of adding more?

It’s fully booked for the next two months, which tells us the need was there. We’re talking about it. For now, we’re keeping it to the one evening to make sure it’s sustainable for the staff. But yes, the response has been very positive.

We’re about out of time. My thanks again to Oriel, Flora, Ines, Rosa, and Alma for sharing. These stories—of repair, access, preparation, and care—are what weave our communities together, festival season or not. The recording will be in the network library by tomorrow. Goodnight, everyone.
